land.text: the Nationalist zone of the civil war, whose rebel regime Franco headed from 1 October 1936

predecessors.note: Francoist Spain page: 'On 1 October 1936, Franco was formally recognised as Caudillo of Spain'; the Cliopatria row starts in 1939 and the infobox gives the victory as 1 April 1939.

land.text: the last Republican territory, conquered in the first months of 1939

predecessors.note: The Republic ended on 1 April 1939 (Second Spanish Republic dossier of eu-21-c).

land.text: Spain proper and the Canary Islands, under King Juan Carlos I

successors.note: Francoist Spain page: 'With the death of Franco on 20 November 1975, Juan Carlos became the King of Spain'; the infobox gives the proclamation of Juan Carlos I as 22 November 1975.

land.text: the Spanish Sahara, whose administration Spain gave up after the Madrid Accords of 14 November 1975

successors.note: The share that went to Mauritania is not on the pages opened (Mauritania's dossier by af-08 dates it 1976).

capitals.name: Madrid
capitals.note: Infobox capital Madrid; during the war 'Salamanca served as the de facto Nationalist capital' and 'administrative functions were moved to Burgos' (see spanish-nationalists).

rulers.name: Francisco Franco
rulers.title: Caudillo (head of state)
rulers.note: 'On 1 October 1936, Franco was formally recognised as Caudillo of Spain'; 'In 1969 Franco designated Juan Carlos as heir'; Franco died on 20 November 1975.

keyframe_review.note: 854,092 km2 for 1939 against the infobox's 856,045 km2 for 1940 (ratio 1.00). The shape is mainland Spain with the Balearic and Canary Islands, northern Morocco, Ifni, Cape Juby, the Spanish Sahara and Spanish Guinea. For January to March the same land was still being conquered (see spanish-nationalists_1939).

854,137 km2 against the infobox's 856,045 km2 for 1940 (ratio 1.00). Tangier (382 km2 on the Tangier International Zone page) is not in the shape; its Spanish occupation from 14 June 1940 is a ledger event, not part of the keyframe. Valid 1940-1941.
853,963 km2: the same land as 1940, a 170 km2 difference that is outline noise. Valid 1942.

keyframe_review.note: Valid for 1945-1955 only. Cliopatria keeps the 854,238 km2 shape to 1957, but Spanish Morocco (about 20,000 km2 on the Spanish Morocco page) 'became part of independent Morocco on 7 April 1956', so 1956-1957 needs the new keyframe francoist-spain_1956. Cape Juby was still Spanish until 1 April 1958. keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Spain without the northern protectorate from 7 April 1956 ('The northern zone became part of independent Morocco on 7 April 1956'); Cape Juby (Tarfaya), Ifni, the Sahara and Spanish Guinea are kept. About 20,000 km2 lighter than the Cliopatria 1945 shape, close to the 1958 shape's 40,025 km2 drop once Cape Juby is added.

814,213 km2: the shape without northern Morocco and without Cape Juby. 'Spain finally ceded its southern zone through the Treaty of Angra de Cintra on 1 April 1958'; the Spanish Sahara page: Spain 'united the territories of Saguia el-Hamra and Río de Oro to form the overseas province of Spanish Sahara' in 1958 'while ceding the province of the Cape Juby strip ... in the same year to Morocco'. Valid 1958-1959.
813,781 km2: the 1958 land, a 430 km2 outline difference. Valid 1960.

keyframe_review.note: Valid 1961-1967 only. The shape still holds Spanish Guinea (Equatorial Guinea, 104 cells) and Ifni to 1972, but 'On 12 October 1968, Spain conceded the independence of the Republic of Equatorial Guinea' (the infobox says 13 October) and Ifni was ceded by the treaty of 5 January 1969 (Spanish Morocco page). 1968 and 1969-1975 are covered by francoist-spain_1968 and francoist-spain_1973. [orchestrator 2 Nov 2026: from/to set to 1961..1967 from this entry's own 'Valid 1961-1967 only'; without them the compiler drew the shape for all its Cliopatria years, overlapping the next keyframe (window p1100-p1199 report)]

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for 1968: the 1961 shape without Spanish Guinea, independent as Equatorial Guinea on 12 October 1968; Ifni is still Spanish until 5 January 1969.

correction.text: unchanged shape; it holds from 1969 to the end in November 1975

keyframe_review.note: 784,334 km2: Spain, the Canary Islands, northern Morocco's remaining enclaves and the Spanish Sahara (about 272,000 km2 on the Spanish Sahara page), without Guinea and Ifni. The shape is right but starts in 1969, not 1973: Spanish Guinea left in October 1968 and Ifni on 5 January 1969. It ends with the Spanish Sahara still inside, which is right until the Madrid Accords of 14 November 1975.

region.text: the whole of Spain and its colonies: the Cliopatria 1939 shape

ledger.note: 1 April 1939: Franco's victory makes Spain a single Francoist state. The infobox gives 'Nationalist victory: 1 April 1939'; the regime's formal head, 'Caudillo of Spain', dated from 1 October 1936 (see spanish-nationalists).

region.text: the international city of Tangier and its zone (382 km2)

ledger.note: 14 June 1940: Spain occupies Tangier. 'Spanish troops occupied Tangier on 14 June 1940, the same day Paris fell to the Germans'; the zone's Committee of Control and Legislative Assembly were abolished on 3 November 1940 and 'Tangier was effectively annexed to the Spanish Protectorate of Morocco on 23 November 1940'.

region.text: the international city of Tangier and its zone

ledger.note: October 1945: Spain leaves Tangier. 'A quadripartite conference ... met in Paris in August 1945' and 'The Anglo-French Agreement entered into force on 11 October 1945', restoring the zone's international institutions; the page does not say on what day the Spanish troops left.

1947: Spain is declared a kingdom without a king. 'On 26 July 1947, Spain was declared a kingdom, but no monarch was designated' (the infobox gives the Law of Succession as 6 July 1947, the page does not explain the difference); no monarch was named until 1969, when Franco designated Juan Carlos as heir. The state, its colour and its land do not change.

region.text: the Spanish protectorate in northern Morocco, about 20,000 km2 with its capital at Tetuán

ledger.note: 7 April 1956: Spain gives up the northern protectorate. 'The northern zone became part of independent Morocco on 7 April 1956, shortly after France relinquished its protectorate'; Spain 'retroceded the territory to the newly independent kingdom' and kept the plazas de soberanía (Ceuta and Melilla).

region.text: Ifni and the Cape Juby strip, where the Moroccan attack of the Ifni War fell

ledger.note: 23 November 1957: the Ifni War opens. Ifni War page: 'On 23 November 1957, two villages on the outskirts of Sidi Ifni, Goulimine and Bouizakarne, were occupied' (infobox '23 November 1957 – 30 June 1958'). The Spanish Morocco page calls it 'the 1958 war': 'During the 1958 war, Spanish control of Ifni was reduced to the perimeter of the city itself' and 'Morocco gained Tarfaya during the Ifni War'. [Reviewer eu-21-d: year corrected from 1958 to 1957-11.]

region.text: the Cape Juby (Tarfaya) strip, the southern zone of the protectorate that Spain still held in 1957 and the 1958 shape no longer has

ledger.note: 1 April 1958: Spain cedes the Cape Juby strip. 'Spain finally ceded its southern zone through the Treaty of Angra de Cintra on 1 April 1958, after the short Ifni War'; the Spanish Sahara page confirms the 'Cape Juby strip' went to Morocco in 1958. The page's 1956 passage says Spain kept Cape Juby until then.

the Cape Juby (Tarfaya) strip, the southern zone of the protectorate that Spain still held in 1957 and the 1958 shape no longer has

region.text: Ifni and the Cape Juby strip

ledger.note: 1 April 1958: the Ifni War ends with the Treaty of Angra de Cintra; Spain keeps Ifni and the Sahara.

region.text: Spanish Guinea: Fernando Po, Río Muni and the islands

ledger.note: 12 October 1968: Spanish Guinea becomes Equatorial Guinea. 'On 12 October 1968, Spain conceded the independence of the Republic of Equatorial Guinea' (the infobox says 13 October). It had been an overseas province from 1959 and autonomous from 1963.

region.text: the exclave of Ifni, the part of the 1961-1972 shape that the 1973 shape lacks once Spanish Guinea is taken out

ledger.note: 5 January 1969: Spain cedes Ifni. 'On 5 January 1969 Morocco and Spain signed the treaty ceding Ifni to Morocco.' The Spanish Sahara page agrees: 'In 1969, Spain ceded Ifni to Morocco, but continued to retain Spanish Sahara.'

region.text: the Spanish Sahara (Saguia el-Hamra and Río de Oro), about 272,000 km2

ledger.note: 14 November 1975: Spain agrees to leave the Sahara. The infobox gives the Madrid Accords as 14 November 1975; the page says only that 'Spain withdrew its forces and citizens' and that a 'mass demonstration of 350,000 Moroccans' advanced in the 'winter of 1975'; the Francoist Spain page: 'Only in 1975, with the Green March and the military occupation, did Morocco take control'. The division between Morocco and Mauritania and the day Spanish rule ended (1976) are not on the pages opened.

region.text: Spain proper and the Canary Islands, which the monarchy keeps

ledger.note: 20 November 1975: Franco dies and the regime ends. 'With the death of Franco on 20 November 1975, Juan Carlos became the King of Spain'; the infobox gives 22 November 1975 for the proclamation of Juan Carlos I.

wars.name: Ifni War

union.text: the exclave of Ifni, the part of the 1961-1972 shape that the 1973 shape lacks once Spanish Guinea is taken out

zones.text: Ifni and the Cape Juby strip

wars.outcome: Spain lost the Cape Juby strip by the Treaty of Angra de Cintra (1 April 1958) and was reduced in Ifni to the city's perimeter; Ifni itself was ceded on 5 January 1969.
wars.note: The page dates the war 1958 only and, in its 1956 passage, says Spain still held Cape Juby, which conflicts with 'Morocco gained Tarfaya during the Ifni War'. The Francoist Spain page says Ifni and the Sahara became provinces in 1958 but dates no war. Reviewer eu-21-d: the Ifni War page dates the war '23 November 1957 – 30 June 1958' and hostilities ceased in April 1958 with the Treaty of Angra de Cintra, so the war starts in 1957.

wars.name: Green March and Madrid Accords
wars.outcome: Spain agreed on 14 November 1975 to withdraw from the Sahara; Morocco took control after the Green March.
wars.note: The page does not date the Green March (6 November 1975 is not on it) and names no Mauritanian share.

certainty.note: Spain's land frontiers and provincial boundaries, the 1956 and 1958 Moroccan cessions and the 1968 and 1969 handovers rest on treaties or independence acts; the interior borders of the Spanish Sahara and the Cape Juby strip were colonial lines and are approximate.

notes:
Page budget (up to 5) spent on Francoist Spain, Spanish Morocco, Tangier International Zone, Spanish Sahara and Spanish Guinea.

Cliopatria corrections: (1) the 1945 shape (to 1957) still holds northern Morocco after its retrocession on 7 April 1956; (2) the 1961 shape (to 1972) still holds Spanish Guinea (independent 12 October 1968) and Ifni (ceded 5 January 1969): the loss appears only in the 1973 shape; (3) the Cape Juby drop is right (1958) and needs no change; (4) Tangier is not in any shape and is drawn as an occupation 1940-1945 (the Tangier International Zone dossier of af-08 records the same pair from its side). The Spanish Sahara stays in the 1973 shape through November 1975; Cliopatria's Kingdom of Spain shape of 1976 lacks it, so the Saharan loss is dated to the Madrid Accords of 14 November 1975 while the Moroccan dossier dates the end of the contest to 1976.

Not settled: when the Sahara, Ifni, Cape Juby and Spanish Guinea were first held by the Nationalists (see spanish-nationalists notes); whether to read the 1947 'kingdom' as a rename (it changes nothing on the map); the Ifni War's start month (the page dates it 1958 only); the Mauritanian share of the Sahara (Mauritania's dossier has it as 1976); the name of the successor of the Spanish Sahara, which is not a state in Cliopatria until the Sahrawi Republic (1976).
Region names: Tarfaya, Ifni and Sidi Ifni are not in the gazetteer; the Cape Juby and Ifni regions are therefore written as differences between Cliopatria shapes. 'W. Sahara' is the Natural Earth country for the Spanish Sahara.
